Atlas replaces the nightly spreadsheet reconciliation that the finance team does by hand. It pulls invoices from the ERP, matches them against bank statement lines, and flags what doesn't match. The finance ops team (Neha's team, 6 people) spends about 3 days every month-end on this today; the goal is to bring that under half a day.
I'm the tech lead. Team: Rohan (backend), Farah (backend), Tushar (frontend, 50%), Divya (QA). PM is Karan. Stakeholder on the finance side is Neha Joshi.
Import invoices from the ERP's export API every night (only the India entity for v1)
Import bank statements from HDFC and ICICI as MT940 files dropped on SFTP
Matching rules: exact amount + reference number first, then amount + date within 3 days, then fuzzy on vendor name
A review screen where finance ops approve or reject suggested matches
An audit trail of who approved what — the auditors asked for this explicitly
Out of scope for v1: multi-currency, the Singapore entity, automatic posting back to the ERP. We only suggest; a person approves.

Django + DRF service with Postgres, Celery workers for the imports and the matching run. Matching is a batch job, not real time: finance wants a stable list in the morning, not one that shifts while they work. Each run is stored with its inputs so we can replay it when someone disputes a match.

The MT940 parser is the part I trust least. Both banks bend the format: HDFC puts the UTR in field 86, ICICI sometimes splits it across two lines. We keep raw lines alongside parsed ones so we can re-parse after a fix without asking the bank for the files again.

Idempotency: every import is keyed by (bank, statement date, file hash). Re-dropping the same file is a no-op. We learned this the hard way on the previous project where a retried job doubled a month of entries.

Hard constraint: nothing goes live during the month-end close window (last 3 working days + first 5 working days of the month). Neha was very firm on this.
ICICI has changed their MT940 layout twice this year without notice. Mitigation: keep raw lines, alert on parse failures, a fixture file per bank per variant in the tests.
The export API allows 100 requests a minute and the full invoice pull is ~40k invoices. Mitigation: incremental pulls by modified date, backfill on weekends.

If the first week's matches are wrong, finance will go back to the spreadsheet and never return. Mitigation: start with exact matches only in the beta; turn on fuzzy matching after they've seen it be right.
and the review screen is the thing finance actually sees. If his other project slips, the screen slips. Raised with Karan; fallback is Farah picks up the screen in Sprint 4.

Mummy ka tarika — slow and patient. Serves 4.
1 cup sabut urad (whole black gram), 1/4 cup rajma — raat bhar bhigo ke rakhna (soak overnight)
2 tbsp butter + 2 tbsp ghee, 1/4 cup fresh cream
1 onion, 3 tomatoes pureed, 1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste
Kashmiri lal mirch, garam masala, kasuri methi, salt
Pressure cook the soaked dal and rajma with salt for 5–6 whistles, then 20 minutes on low. It should be completely soft, mash kar sako.
Ghee mein onion golden hone tak bhuno, then ginger-garlic paste, then the tomato puree. Cook till the oil separates.
Add the spices, then the dal. Simmer on the lowest flame for at least 45 minutes, stirring and mashing a little. Paani add karte rehna.
Finish with butter, cream and crushed kasuri methi.
Tip from Mummy: for the dhaba taste, put a hot coal in a small katori of ghee on top and cover for 2 minutes (dhungar).

Deep work is professional activity done in distraction-free concentration that pushes your cognitive abilities to their limit. It creates new value, improves your skill, and is hard to replicate. The ability to do it is becoming rare at exactly the time it's becoming valuable — so the few who cultivate it will thrive.

His formula: high-quality work produced = time spent × intensity of focus. Attention residue is the killer: when you switch from task A to task B, part of your attention stays on A. Checking email 'for a second' costs far more than a second.

Shallow work is non-cognitively demanding, logistical work, often done while distracted — email, meetings, Slack, status updates. It doesn't create much new value and anyone could do it. Newport's point is not that it's useless, but that it expands to fill the day if you let it. He suggests asking: how long would it take to train a smart graduate with no experience in my field to do this task? If the answer is a few weeks, it's shallow.
He recommends budgeting shallow work explicitly: agree with your manager on a percentage (he suggests 30–50% for most knowledge workers) and hold to it.
Choose a depth philosophy — monastic, bimodal, rhythmic or journalistic. Rhythmic (same time every day) is the realistic one for me.
Don't reach for the phone the moment you're idle; otherwise the brain can't concentrate when you need it to. Schedule internet time rather than scheduling offline time.
— or at least apply the craftsman approach: keep a tool only if its benefits substantially outweigh its costs for the things that matter most.
Schedule every minute of the workday in blocks. End the day with a shutdown ritual: review tasks, plan tomorrow, say 'shutdown complete'.
9:30–12:00 is a no-meetings, no-Slack block three days a week. Blocked on the calendar as 'Atlas design'.
